t: The curved one. The horn must be bent and not straight.
And although the Torah did not specify a blast with a shofar on Rosh Hashanah. For the Torah did not specify with which instrument one is to sound the teruah on Rosh Hashanah.
Concerning the Jubilee it says. Concerning the mitzvah of blowing on Yom Kippur of the Jubilee year (see Hilchot Shemitah VeYovel 10:10).
And from tradition. The tradition of the Sages.
From the sides. Of the one blowing the shofar.
For the mitzvah of the day is with the shofar. And the trumpets are only for honor and splendor.
Before the King, the Lord. In the Temple.
Of idolatry. Which is idolatrous property and forbidden to benefit from, but there is no mitzvah to destroy it (R. Y. Kafih and Yad Peshutah).

And of an apostate city. A city most of whose inhabitants are idol worshippers, all of whose property must be burned (Hilchot Avodah Zarah 4:6); the shofar is considered burned and as if lacking the required measure explained below, halacha 5 (see Hilchot Shabbat 17:12; and see also below 8:1).

A stolen shofar that he blew, he has fulfilled his obligation etc.. And it is not disqualified as a mitzvah performed through a transgression (see below 8:1), because the mitzvah is fulfilled by the sound of the blast, which involves no theft, and not by the body of the shofar.
Of a burnt offering. An animal that was consecrated as a burnt offering.

For sound is not subject to the law of me'ilah. For the prohibition of me'ilah does not apply to things with no substance, such as sound (Hilchot Me'ilah 5:16), and therefore this is not a mitzvah performed through a transgression.
And if you say, but does he not benefit from hearing the sound. And how did he fulfill his obligation with something forbidden for benefit.
Mitzvot were not given for benefit. And although he benefits by hearing the sound of the shofar, the fulfillment of mitzvot is not included in the category of benefit.
Therefore one who is prohibited by vow from benefit etc.. One who vowed not to benefit from a certain shofar is permitted to blow it for the sake of a mitzvah, since this is not benefit.
We do not desecrate the festival for it. In order to fulfill the mitzvah of the shofar.
Even for something that is only a shevut. That is forbidden by rabbinic decree.
He does not climb a tree. For the Sages forbade this lest he pluck (Hilchot Shabbat 21:6).
And he does not swim on the surface of the water. For the Sages forbade this lest he repair a boat (ibid. 23:5).
And needless to say, we do not cut it. For this action is sometimes forbidden by the Torah (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Rosh Hashanah 4:8).

For blowing the shofar is a positive commandment, and the festival is a positive and a negative commandment. On a festival there is a positive commandment to rest from work and a negative commandment not to do work, and the positive commandment of the shofar does not override a negative and positive commandment (for this rule see also Hilchot Yom Tov 3:8, Hilchot Yibum VeChalitzah 6:11, Hilchot Shechitah 13:19, Hilchot Nezirut 7:15, Hilchot Gezelah VaAvedah 11:18).
To clean it. To clean it and improve its sound; this is not considered the work of repair that is forbidden on a festival.
And he may not put urine into it. Urine, even though its sourness helps to clean and repair the shofar.
So that mitzvot not be degraded by it. For this principle see also Hilchot Shechitah 14:16.
And it is visible on this side and that side. It protrudes outward from his palm on both sides of it.

If the required measure remains in it etc.. If from the mouthpiece of the shofar to the crack there is the measure of a shofar, it is valid, for we consider only the part of the shofar that did not crack, and the rest as if it were cut off.
If he plugged it with something not of its kind. With another material that is not an animal's horn.
If most of it remained whole. Most of the shofar was not perforated.
And the holes that were plugged did not impair the blast. For before the holes were plugged, the blast was heard properly (Hagahot Maimoniyot, and see Piskim VeShitot).

He drilled it through its bone, it is valid. The animal's horn is composed of a bone ("zachrut") surrounded by horny material. If he did not remove the bone from the outer horn but drilled a hole through the bone from end to end, it is valid.

For one kind does not interpose with its own kind. The bone and the outer horn are considered one kind, and therefore the bone does not constitute an addition or interposition between the horn and the hollow of the shofar into which one blows (for this principle see below 7:12, Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 1:21).
He added anything to it. He lengthened the shofar.
Or at the place where the mouth is placed. Even on the outside, since there is an interposition between the mouth of the one blowing and the shofar.
He covered it on the outside. Not at the place where the mouth is placed.
He widened the narrow part and narrowed the wide part. He reduced and narrowed the wide end of the shofar so that it would serve as a mouthpiece, and enlarged and widened the mouthpiece.
He scraped it. He scraped the shofar and removed from it a layer or several layers of its thickness.
He left it standing on its outer skin. The thinnest layer.
Thick or thin. Low or high.
Echo. A resonance.
And freed slaves. Freed Canaanite slaves, who have the status of Israelites in every respect (Hilchot Issurei Biah 12:17).

Women and slaves... are exempt. For women are exempt from positive commandments that are time-bound (Hilchot Avodah Zarah 12:3), and slaves are exempt from positive commandments from which women are exempt (Hilchot Chagigah 2:1).
One who is half slave and half free. One who had two partner owners and one of them freed him, or whose owner freed half of him (see Hilchot Avadim 7:4).

And a tumtum. One whose sexual organs are covered and it is not apparent whether he is male or female; if his sexual organs are revealed and he is found to be male, his law is that of a definite male, and if found to be female, she is a female (Hilchot Ishut 2:25). [Note: in the Commentary on the Mishnah the Rambam vocalizes this word tumtom.]
And an androginos. One who has both male and female sexual organs, and is defined as a doubtful male, doubtful female whose sex there is no way to determine (ibid. 2:24).
An androginos may fulfill the obligation of his own kind. Another androginos, since all androginoses have the same law, being defined as doubtful male, doubtful female.

And he does not fulfill the obligation of one who is not his kind. He cannot fulfill the obligation of one who is a definite male, since one obligated by doubt cannot fulfill the obligation of one definitely obligated.

A tumtum does not fulfill the obligation of his own kind etc.. For every tumtum is a doubt in his own right (and when the membrane covering his sexual organs is torn his identity will become clear), and it is possible that this tumtum is a female and cannot fulfill the obligation of another tumtum who is male.

For his aspect of slavery does not fulfill the obligation for his aspect of freedom. For when he blows, his aspect of slavery participates in the blowing, and that aspect is exempt from the blowing and cannot fulfill the obligation of his aspect of freedom, which is obligated in the blowing.
One who is engaged in blowing the shofar in order to learn. He blows the shofar in order to learn how to blow, and does not intend it for the mitzvah of the shofar.
Until he intends etc.. For both the listener and the blower must intend to fulfill the mitzvah.

Even though the blower does not intend for so-and-so... and does not know him. That he did not have in mind to fulfill the obligation of that particular person, and did not even know that he was hearing his blowing.

Even though the blowing is a shevut etc.. Although the prohibition of blowing on Shabbat is only rabbinic (see Hilchot Shabbat 23:4), and by law the blowing of the shofar, which is a positive Torah commandment, should override a rabbinic prohibition, nevertheless we do not blow because of a special rabbinic decree.

And carry it four cubits etc.. And this is work forbidden by the Torah on pain of stoning (see ibid. 12:8), and because of the concern about this prohibition they decreed that the positive commandment of the shofar be set aside (for a similar decree see below 7:13, and Hilchot Megillah 1:13).
Children who have not reached the age of training. The age of training in mitzvot.

On a Shabbat that is not the festival of Rosh Hashanah. But on a Shabbat that is Rosh Hashanah, children are prevented from blowing, so that people will not err and say that it is permitted to blow on Rosh Hashanah that falls on Shabbat (Maggid Mishneh; and the Kesef Mishneh explained that on a Shabbat that is the festival of Rosh Hashanah, all the more so we do not prevent them from blowing).

So that they will learn. To blow the shofar when they are grown. But once they have reached the age of training, they are prevented, since it is forbidden to blow on Shabbat and festivals because of shevut.
And an adult may engage with them... on the festival. On the festival of Rosh Hashanah, on which the mitzvah is to blow.
The Great Court in Jerusalem. The Great Sanhedrin of seventy-one judges.
As long as the court is sitting. While the court session is convened.
Which was within the boundary of Jerusalem. Within two thousand cubits of the city, so that it is permitted to walk from it to Jerusalem on Shabbat.
And provided that it is ordained in the Land. That its judges received appointment to judge in the Land of Israel (for the details of ordination see Hilchot Sanhedrin 4:1-4).
In a court that sanctified the month. That fixed the new month on the basis of witnesses, and this is done only by an ordained court in the Land of Israel (Hilchot Kiddush HaChodesh 5:1).
But outside the court they do not blow. Even if the judges are sitting at that time within the court.
Zealous. Careful with mitzvot.

At this time when we observe two days in the Diaspora. For outside the Land of Israel all festivals are observed for two festival days, as was the practice when they sanctified the month on the basis of sighting (Hilchot Kiddush HaChodesh 5:5-6).

Because teruah is stated etc.. The word "teruah" is mentioned in the Torah three times in connection with the mitzvah of blowing on Rosh Hashanah and on the Jubilee (Leviticus 23:24; 25:9; Numbers 29:1).

And every teruah has a plain blast before it and a plain blast after it. Every teruah sound (which is a series of several broken sounds, as explained in the next halacha) must have a continuous, smooth blast blown before it and after it.
And from tradition. The tradition of the Sages.

That all the teruot of the seventh month are one. Their law is the same. And since in the combined context of both, teruah is mentioned three times, one must blow three teruot at each of these times, that is, nine blasts.
Because of the length of the years and the multitude of exiles. Because of the many years that have passed and the upheavals of exile.

Whether it is the wailing etc.. The wailing sound that is customarily made in a time of distress, which is a long trembling sound (Siddur of Rav Saadia Gaon, and see Migdal Oz citing Rabbi Yitzchak Gei'at).
Or the groaning etc.. Like a person's groans, which are a series of several broken sounds.
Or both of them as one. That the teruah is composed of the two sounds: the sound of groaning together with the sound of wailing that follows it.
Therefore we do all of it, the groaning and the wailing. Groaning, wailing, and groaning and wailing in sequence. In each of these ways they blow three times.

And the wailing is what we call teruah. Although we are in doubt as to what the sound of the "teruah" mentioned in the Torah is (groaning or wailing), we customarily call the wailing by the name teruah and the groaning by the name shevarim.

It turns out that the order of the blasts is as follows etc.. By strict law one would need to blow three times: tekiah, teruah, tekiah. Because of the doubt about what the teruah is, we blow: tekiah, shevarim, teruah, tekiah (tashrat) three times; tekiah, shevarim, tekiah (tashat) three times; tekiah, teruah, tekiah (tarat) three times.
It turns out that the number of blasts is thirty. Twelve blasts in the tashrat series, nine in the tashat series, and nine in the tarat series.

The measure of a teruah is like two tekiot etc.. It appears that in the Rambam's view there is no fixed measure for the blasts, but they are measured relative to one another. According to this the teruah must be the length of two tekiot as blown by that person, while the total measure of the three shevarim should be no more than the measure of a teruah, so that each shever is not the length of a tekiah (based on Yad Peshutah, and see the commentators who explained in various ways).
If he blew a tekiah, a teruah etc.. If he blew a tekiah, a teruah and a tekiah, and in the second tekiah he lengthened it to twice the duration of the first tekiah.

We do not say it is counted as two tekiot etc.. We do not count this long tekiah as two tekiot: as the last tekiah of the previous series and as the first tekiah of the next series (so that he could then immediately sound a teruah without blowing a tekiah); rather he must pause, and then blow the first tekiah of the next series.
At any time. Without limit.
He heard one tekiah at this hour etc.. He heard the blasts not consecutively but with an interval of time between each one.
Provided that he hears each series in its proper order. For one must hear the blasts of each series (tashat/tarat/tashrat) in the correct order: tekiah, teruah, tekiah.
For all of them are one mitzvah. One single, complete obligation.
He heard nine blasts. The nine blasts required by the Torah (three series of tekiah, teruah, tekiah).
As one. . All at once.
A tekiah from this one, a teruah from that one, and a tekiah from a third, one after another. That is, in the correct order, and not simultaneously, but each blast from a different person.
With interruptions. With pauses.
Until he hears all nine blasts. Those required by the basic Torah law (and in our time thirty blasts because of the doubt, as above, halacha 4).

According to the order of the blessings. Of the Musaf Amidah of Rosh Hashanah (and of Yom Kippur in the Jubilee), which has nine blessings (see Hilchot Tefillah 2:6, 2:8; Seder HaTefillot, middle blessings of Shabbatot and festivals, 14-16).
And Malchuyot. This is the fourth blessing, after the three blessings fixed every day; it concerns God's kingship in the world, and in this blessing one also mentions the sanctity of the day.
And he blows three. A teruah (in whichever form), with a tekiah before it and after it.
Zichronot. . This is the fifth blessing, and it concerns God remembering the deeds of the world, the binding of Isaac and His covenant with the patriarchs.
Shofarot. . This is the sixth blessing, and it concerns the proclamation of God's kingship with the shofar, and His revelation in this sound.

Avodah, Hoda'ah and Birkat Kohanim. The last three blessings: "Retzeh," "Modim," and "Sim Shalom," which is recited after the Priestly Blessing (see Mishnah Tamid 5:1 and the Commentary on the Mishnah there).
They hold each other back. . That if he did not say all of them, he has not fulfilled his obligation at all.
Something like the blessing. . Something of the substance of the blessing.
Tehillim. Psalms.
And one from the Torah completes it. He concludes with a verse from the Torah (and completes the count of ten verses).
And if he completed with a Prophet. If he said the tenth verse from the books of the Prophets.
And if he said a verse etc.. That is, even one verse from each section of the Tanakh; he has also fulfilled his obligation after the fact.
And he said a verse of Torah and stopped. That is, he mentioned only one verse from the Torah, and concluded his blessing with that without mentioning further verses.
He need not do anything more. To go back and bless a second time, for he has fulfilled his obligation.
Of punishment. Calamities.
And He remembered that they are flesh. God remembered that the people of Israel are material creatures whose end is to pass away.

And with outpoured wrath I will be king over you. So prophesied Ezekiel, that the Children of Israel did not want to accept God's kingship over them but asked to be like the other nations, but against their will God will reign over them and in fury.
Blow the shofar in Gibeah, the trumpet in Ramah. To warn the people of the enemy's armies.
And not the remembrance of an individual. A remembrance that deals with a private person.
Remember me, O Lord, with the favor of Your people. So the psalmist prays, that God remember him at the time He shows His favor and love to His people.
Remember me, my God, for good. So Nehemiah prays, that God remember for him the good he did for the people of Israel.
And pekidot are not like zichronot. The root p-k-d is not identical to remembrance, and therefore verses containing this root cannot be said as zichronot verses.
I have surely remembered you. The words of God to Moses when He appeared to him at the bush and informed him of Israel's redemption from Egypt.
And he may. And he is permitted.
Punishment of the nations of the world. Evils and calamities concerning the other nations.
The Lord reigns, let the peoples tremble. When God reveals His kingship, the peoples will tremble (be afraid) from fear of Him.

Remember, O Lord, against the children of Edom the day of Jerusalem. Remember, O God, the conduct of the Edomites on the day of Jerusalem's destruction, when they rejoiced at its misfortune and even wanted it to be destroyed to its foundations (and therefore we pray that they receive their recompense).

And the Lord God will blow the shofar and go in the whirlwinds of the south. When God reveals His Presence to fight alongside Israel against their enemies, He will blow the shofar and go like a strong southern storm wind (whirlwinds of the south) to take vengeance on Israel's enemies.
You were shown to know. The people of Israel saw and were convinced at the Sinai revelation: "that the Lord is God, there is none besides Him."
Each of these verses is about kingship. All these verses concern God's kingship in the world.
Even though it contains no mention of kingship. Although the root m-l-ch is not explicitly mentioned in it.
And it is like etc.. Their subject and teaching are identical to the verses in which God's kingship is explicitly mentioned, and therefore they may be recited as Malchuyot verses.
And he blows the thirty blasts that we mentioned. Above, halacha 3.
This one who blows etc.. The same ba'al tokea who recites the blessing and blows before Musaf is the one who must also blow during the Musaf prayer.
And he does not speak. The blower is forbidden to speak between the first blasts and the blasts that accompany the order of blessings.
Spoke. Talked.

By law it should have been etc.. By strict law, at the end of each blessing they should have blown one of the series three times (at the end of Malchuyot tashrat, at the end of Zichronot tashat, and at the end of Shofarot tarat), so that in total they would blow thirty sounds, matching the number of blasts blown while seated (R. Y. Kafih, and see Lechem Mishneh).
But an individual etc.. An individual need not be careful about these laws.
And there is no custom in this. That is accepted and binding.
The blasts do not hold back etc.. These are two separate obligations, and if he did only one of them he has fulfilled that obligation, even though he did not do the other.
And he may add to its width even several miles. It is permitted to enlarge it as much as he wishes (the length of a mil is about a kilometer).
Like the shape of gam. Like the shape of the Greek letter gamma, whose form resembles the letter resh.

And he stands it at less than three handbreadths from one of the two walls, and that suffices. He stands the small wall adjacent to one of the walls at a distance of slightly less than three handbreadths from it (since such a distance is not considered a gap, below halacha 15), and thus the total length of the wall together with the gap is about four handbreadths, which is a significant measure of space (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Sukkah 1:1).

The shape of a doorway. Reeds that form the shape of a doorway. It must be placed at the fourth wall so that it will be clear that the entrance of the sukkah is there and not at the open third wall (Yad Peshutah, based on Rabbi Yitzchak Gei'at). Some say it should be placed at the third wall (from the place where he set up a wall a handbreadth wide to the place parallel to the end of the opposite wall), because this wall is not complete and the doorway shape gives it the status of a complete wall (Rabbenu Manoach, and this is the view of the Shulchan Aruch and the Rema - see Piskim VeShitot).
And we already explained in Hilchot Shabbat. 16:19.
Even though it does not reach them. Even though the upper reed does not rest directly on the standing reeds, it is considered the shape of a doorway.
Two walls opposite each other with an open space between them. Two complete walls facing each other, with the area between them completely open.

He makes a wall four handbreadths wide and a little more etc.. In this case the small wall should be made four handbreadths and a bit, so that together with the gap the wall's length is seven handbreadths, which is the width of a valid sukkah.
And he must make it the shape of a doorway. See the previous halacha.

Reeds extending from the sukkah's roofing etc.. When the roofing extends beyond one of the walls but the parallel wall extends and continues together with the roofing, the entire area under the roofing is treated as a sukkah.
Walls that were attached to the roof of the sukkah. They are connected to the roof of the sukkah, but below they do not reach the ground.
If they are three handbreadths above the ground, it is invalid. Since the wall hangs in the air and does not reach the ground, it is not a proper partition.
Provided that the walls are aligned under the edge of the roof. For we see the partition as if it continues upward to the roofing.
He moved the roof away. So that the walls are not aligned under the roof.

He hung a partition etc.. He set up a partition slightly more than four handbreadths high in the middle of the height of the sukkah, so that the partition is less than three handbreadths from the ground and less than three from the roofing, such that the total length of the partition together with the gaps is ten handbreadths.
The ordinary wind. The usual, average wind.
The tree tops. The tops of the trees.
In an ordinary land wind. Which is weaker than the ordinary wind at sea.
And one may go up to it on a festival. It is permitted to go up and enter it on a festival.

Because it is forbidden to climb a tree or onto an animal. For they decreed against these things, lest he pluck a branch while climbing the tree or cut a branch to lead the animal he is riding (see Hilchot Shabbat 21:6, 21:9).

Some of the walls were made by human hands and some were trees. He built his sukkah at a height, and part of the sukkah's floor and walls rests and leans on trees, and part rests and leans on supports made by human hands (Rabbenu Manoach).

Any that if etc.. If the sukkah is built so that if the trees were removed the sukkah would not stand, one may not go up and enter this sukkah on a festival (because he would be using a tree), but if it would remain stable even without the trees, it is permitted.
Like a hut. The walls slant diagonally and meet at the top, in the shape of a triangle.

Or he leaned the top of the sukkah wall against the wall. One wall slants diagonally and leans on a wall. In these cases the sukkah is invalid because there is no clear distinction between the sukkah's roof and its walls.
And if it had a roof of even a handbreadth etc.. Since there is one handbreadth that is distinctly roof or wall, it is valid.
If its perimeter etc.. If within the circumference of the circle one can fit a square of seven by seven handbreadths, it is valid.

He roofed over an akhsadrah. A sort of open space between houses, part of which is roofed, and he placed roofing beyond the end of the akhsadrah's ceiling, so that on two sides it is adjacent to the walls of the houses and on its third side it is adjacent to the akhsadrah's ceiling.
That has doorposts. Pillars at the edge of the akhsadrah that hold up the ceiling.

Whether they were visible from inside etc.. Whether these doorposts protrude toward the inside of the akhsadrah area and are visible from within, or protrude outside the area of the akhsadrah and are not visible from within, the sukkah is valid. Although it has only two parallel walls, since the roofing between them reaches the edge of the akhsadrah's ceiling, and the edge of the ceiling is delimited by the doorposts, one can say that the edge of the ceiling descends downward and constitutes a partition ("the edge of the ceiling descends and seals"; see also Hilchot Shabbat 16:7, 17:35).

And the middle of the akhsadrah has no wall and the opposite side has no doorposts. For the sukkah has only two walls, on the sides, while in the middle of the akhsadrah, where the middle wall should have been, there is no wall at all, and on the opposite side (the end of the roofed akhsadrah) there are no doorposts that could make the ceiling count as a wall.

An alley that has a lechi. A street open on both sides ("a through alley"), which on one side has the shape of a doorway and on the other a small post near its opening ("lechi"); in this way it is permitted to carry in it on Shabbat (Hilchot Shabbat 17:3).

A well that has pasin. A water well around which they built small corner-like structures at the four corners of its area, and thus it is permitted to draw from it on Shabbat for the animals of the pilgrims (see ibid. 17:27-30).

This is a valid sukkah for that Shabbat within the festival etc.. Although generally a lechi and pasin are not valid as walls for a sukkah, since on Shabbat they are treated as partitions with regard to carrying, they are also considered partitions with regard to the walls of the sukkah.
He planted four posts etc.. He planted four posts at the corners of the roof of the house and placed roofing on them.
Since the roofing is on the edge of the roof. Since the edge of the roofing is exactly parallel to the edge of the roof.
And we see the partitions etc.. As if the walls of the house extend upward to the roofing, and they are considered the walls of the sukkah (see above, halacha 4).
Even though the open parts exceed the standing parts. Even though most of the area of the walls is not built but consists of voids and gaps.
Provided that there is no opening greater than ten. Cubits.
It must not be etc.. The sukkah is not disqualified by this, but most of the area of the walls must be built and the gaps must be the minority (compare Hilchot Shabbat 16:16).
Whose space is higher than twenty cubits. Whose inner space is higher than twenty cubits, which is the maximum height of a sukkah (above, halacha 1).
And he reduced it with cushions and pillows. He placed cushions and pillows on its floor and reduced the height of the sukkah's space.
It is not a reduction, even if he nullified them. This is not considered as reducing its space, even if he nullified these cushions in his mind and wanted them to be considered merely ground.
But with plain earth. He placed earth without specifying that he nullifies it and considers it part of the ground.
And the tips. The ends of the roofing branches.

If their shade is greater than their sun etc.. If even without the roofing that is higher than twenty the sukkah is properly covered by the tips and the shade is greater than the sun, it is valid (see below 5:19).
He built a platform etc.. A sukkah higher than twenty cubits that has three walls, and he built in it a raised place to reduce its height (see the illustrations on the next page).
Opposite the middle wall across its whole length. Along the entire length of the sukkah's middle wall (so that the platform is adjacent to three walls).
The measure of the width of a sukkah. Seven by seven handbreadths.
From the side. Along one of the side partitions, so that the platform is adjacent to only two walls.
If from the edge of the platform to the wall etc.. If the platform is more than four cubits from the parallel wall, the sukkah is invalid, since this platform does not have three walls.

Less than four cubits is valid. For we see as if the parallel wall curves and the roofing above it is a continuation of that wall, and it is considered the third wall for this platform (this leniency is called "curved wall" and it works only up to a distance of four cubits, as below 5:14).
In its middle. Not adjacent to any wall but in the center of the sukkah's space.

Less than four cubits is valid, as if the partitions were touching the platform. For we see as if the walls curve, and all the roofing higher than twenty is their continuation, so that in effect this platform has three walls.

A pillar. That is hollow and made of partitions but closed at the top (similar to an upside-down barrel), and from its top to the roofing is less than twenty cubits (unlike a platform, which is solid and has no partitions at all, R. Y. Kafih).
The validity of a sukkah. Seven by seven handbreadths.

It is invalid, since these are not recognizable partitions. Unlike the house on whose roof he planted four posts, where we see as if the walls of the house extend upward to the roofing (above, halacha 11), here the pillar's partitions are not recognizable.
It was less than ten. Handbreadths, which is the minimum height of a sukkah (above, halacha 1).
And dug in it. Dug into the floor of the sukkah.
From the edge of the excavation. From the edge of the hole.
For anything less than three is like attached. As if the gap were not there ("lavud").
As we explained in Hilchot Shabbat. 16:8 and elsewhere.
Of anything. Of any material.
His fellow as a wall. Even another person may serve as a wall.
Without the knowledge of the one who became the wall. That his fellow does not know that he is currently serving as a wall for the sukkah.
But if he did it knowingly, it is forbidden on a festival. Because it resembles building a temporary structure, which is forbidden on a festival, as explained at the end of the halacha.

And likewise he may make a fourth wall with vessels on a festival. He stands various vessels so that they serve as a partition; since he is merely standing the vessels, this is not building, which is forbidden on a festival, and it is permitted to do so when the sukkah already has three walls.

Because it validates the sukkah. For the sukkah would not be valid otherwise, so by standing this wall the structure becomes a valid sukkah, and this resembles making a temporary tent (compare ibid. 16:22-23).
With anything. With any material.
Whose growth is from the earth. From plants.
That was uprooted from the earth. That is no longer attached.
And it does not receive impurity. That is not a vessel that can become impure.
Always. Regularly.
But so that he will not leave the sukkah and go out. Because of the smell or the leaves that fall, but this does not invalidate the sukkah after the fact.
That the tips and leaves not etc.. That the ends of the leaves not hang down below a height of ten handbreadths, so that it will be comfortable to sit there.
He lowered grape leaves and the like until they became a sukkah. He raised vine branches above the sukkah while still attached, so that they would be roofing.
And with mats made for lying on. Mats made to lie on (see below, halacha 6).

With broken vessels and their worn-out pieces. Vessels that broke or garments that wore out to the point that they are no longer considered vessels and are not fit to receive impurity (see Hilchot Kelim chapter 6, and 22:15-27 there).

Since they were etc.. Since at one time they received impurity, there is concern that people will err and permit also vessels that broke in a way that did not purify them from being able to receive impurity.
Because they receive impurity. See Hilchot Tum'at Ochalin 1:1.
Fig branches. Branches of figs.
Vine shoots. Branches of the grapevine.
Palm fronds. Branches of the date palm.

If he trimmed etc.. If there are more branches and leaves that are not used for food and do not receive impurity than the fruits that receive impurity, one may roof with them, and if not, it is forbidden.

With greens that if they dry will crumble and nothing substantial will remain of them. Kinds of leaves and vegetables, for example ones that do not receive impurity (such as those not designated for human food - see there).
Their place etc.. Since they tend to crumble, they are already now considered air and as if there were no roofing at all, and they invalidate at three handbreadths (as below, halacha 20).
With flax stalks. With the flax plant.
That he did not beat them or comb them out. That they did not yet pound the stalks to remove the remains of the woody material, nor comb the fibers to clean and straighten them.
For it is still wood. This flax is still considered as coming from the plant.
Because its form has changed etc.. For it is processed in a way that it is no longer considered a plant.
Siv. A kind of thin mesh growing around the trunk of a palm.
Chelef. Sand willow (chilef hachulot), from which they used to weave ropes and baskets.
For their form still stands. It is evident that they come from plants and their form has not changed very much.
And ropes are not vessels. And they do not receive impurity (see Hilchot Kelim 1:12).
With arrows. With the body of the arrow, which is made of wood, without its metal head.
With male ones. Where the head of the arrow has a protrusion that is inserted into a socket in the body of the arrow.
Valid. By the law of wooden vessels that have no receptacle, which do not receive impurity (see Hilchot Kelim 1:10, 4:1).
With female ones. Where the head of the arrow has a socket into which the body of the arrow is inserted.

Even though it is made to be filled with iron, it is a receptacle. Since when one uses these vessels and roofs with them they have a receptacle (Yad Peshutah in the name of Rabbi Chaim, and compare Hilchot Kelim 2:3).
Reeds. Long thin reeds.
A small one, by default is for lying on. Presumably the intention of its maker was that it would be used for lying on, and therefore it receives impurity.
A large one, by default is for roofing. Presumably the intention of its maker was that it would be used for roofing, and therefore it is not judged to be a vessel and does not receive impurity.
A rim. A raised edge.
Boards. Wooden planks.
Even though they are planed. Smoothed and polished, nevertheless they are not considered vessels that receive impurity.
Lest he sit under the ceiling. And the ceiling is invalid, as explained in the next halacha.
He placed on it one board four handbreadths wide. And the rest of the sukkah is roofed with valid roofing.

Valid, but one may not sleep beneath it. This board is not treated like invalid roofing that invalidates the sukkah if it is four handbreadths wide (below, halacha 14), since the board is not made of invalid material but is forbidden only because of the decree. In any case, one should not sleep under this board because of the decree.
And turned them on their sides so they are not four. He stood the boards on their narrow side.
A ceiling that has no plaster etc.. A ceiling made only of wooden boards, without the stones and mortar on top of them.
Therefore if he loosened the boards and moved the nails. If he undid the connection of the boards to the house by removing the nails from them, and did this for the sake of the sukkah.
If he removed one of every two. If he removed one of every two boards.
This is valid. And he need not loosen the other boards.
A sukkah of gentiles. Made by gentiles.
And a sukkah of animals. Made for the needs of animals.
One who digs into a grain heap. Digs and makes a hole inside a pile of grain.

For he did not stack this heap for shade. When he put down the grain pile he did not do so for it to serve as any kind of shade. And if he dug into the heap, even if he did so for the sake of shade, he performed no new act of making the sukkah (roofing), since this roofing was already standing in its place and he only dug beneath it.

If he made it at the outset etc.. If at the outset, when he put down the heap, he left beneath it a space at least a handbreadth high and seven handbreadths in length and width, one can say that from the beginning this heap was also placed for shade over the space beneath it, and therefore when he increased the height of the space to ten handbreadths, this is a valid sukkah.
Branches. Branches.
Small bundles that were tied for counting. That were tied so as to be arranged in bundles of a fixed number.
One may roof with them. Since they were tied only for counting and he does not intend to leave them tied, there is no concern that he will bring it up to the roof to dry them.
One who cuts the top of a palm with the branches tied in it. He cut the top of the palm tree from which several branches emerge, and this resembles a bundle of branches.
For one who ties a single tree does not make a bundle. For since they are already attached they are considered only one tree, and therefore even if he made a knot, he did not make a bundle.
For it is not made to be carried. For its tying is not strong in this way and may come undone when the bundle is carried.
As if he made it inside the house. And it is invalid.
He raised over it etc.. He raised the leaves of trees and their branches over the sukkah while still attached, placed roofing on top of them, and afterwards cut off the leaves and branches.
If the roofing was much more than they, it is valid. If the valid roofing was more than these branches, it is valid.
So that it be made for the sake of a sukkah. For at first, when they were placed, they were not valid for roofing.

In a small one. . A sukkah whose total area is seven by seven handbreadths (below, halacha 15), and therefore the invalid roofing reduces the minimum measure for validity of the sukkah and it is invalid (but when the invalid roofing is less than three handbreadths it is nullified by the principle of lavud and does not reduce, see above 4:15).

In a large sukkah. A sukkah that has seven by seven handbreadths of valid roofing aside from the invalid roofing (below, halacha 15), and therefore the invalid roofing does not reduce the sukkah below its minimum measure of validity and does not invalidate, unless it has a measure of four handbreadths in the middle (which is a significant measure that invalidates), or is more than four cubits at the side (for less than that it can be considered a "curved wall," as explained shortly).
That was breached in its middle. Part of the ceiling in the middle of the house was missing.

A courtyard surrounded by an akhsadrah. A courtyard surrounded by houses on three sides, with a roofed area along the sides of the courtyard, and he roofed the open area beyond the edge of the akhsadrah's ceiling.
And likewise a large sukkah that was surrounded etc.. On the outer perimeter of the sukkah there is invalid roofing that reaches the walls.

If from the edge etc.. As long as the distance between the roofing and the walls is less than four cubits the sukkah is valid, for we treat the invalid roofing as if it were a continuation of the wall that curves and continues to the place of the valid roofing.
Seven handbreadths by seven handbreadths. . This is the minimum measure for a sukkah (above 4:1).
Any in which there remains etc.. Any sukkah in which there is an area of seven by seven handbreadths of roofing, aside from the invalid roofing.
And there is not in one place etc.. There is not in one continuous place a measure of invalid roofing sufficient to invalidate the sukkah.

And there is not in one place of invalid roofing a width of three handbreadths. In a small sukkah, for if so the sukkah is invalid regardless of the amount of valid roofing (and in a large sukkah the measures are different, as above, halachot 13-14).
Exactly. Precisely.
It is considered as an opening. As if it were not there, and therefore the sukkah is invalid because its sun is greater than its shade (as below, halacha 19).
From above. To protect from the sun and the like.
Beneath it because of what falls. The leaves that fall into the sukkah.
To beautify it. To adorn it.
Sukkah decorations do not reduce its height. Decorations hanging from the ceiling of the sukkah are not considered as reducing its height.
But they reduce its width. If they are adjacent to the walls of the sukkah, they are considered part of the sukkah's structure and reduce its area.

If the sukkah decorations were separated from its roof by four handbreadths or more, it is invalid etc.. That is, the decorations were far from the roofing, and at such a distance they are not nullified to the roofing but are considered a separate thing, and therefore the area under the decoration is invalid for sitting in.
Windows through which the sky is visible. Air holes in the roofing that are not covered at all.
If the entire open space equals the entire covered area. If the uncovered parts are equal in area to the covered part.
And clothing. Garments.
If it is a large sukkah etc.. That invalid roofing does not invalidate it until it is four handbreadths in the middle or four cubits at the side (above, halacha 14).
And if in a small sukkah. In which invalid roofing invalidates at three handbreadths (ibid.).

If most of the roofing had its shade greater than its sun, and a minority had its sun greater than its shade. In most of the area of the sukkah there was more roofing than open air, but in part of its area there was more open air than roofing, the sukkah is valid.
Light. Sparse.
That there not be between the rising and the descending three handbreadths. For then they are considered connected and as if the whole roof were laid evenly (see above 4:15).

And if the width of this rising one was etc.. If the width of the upper roofing is at least a handbreadth, the sukkah is valid even if it is much higher than the rest of the roofing, since we consider it as if it were lowered and made level with the rest of the roofing. But this is only if the upper roofing is directly above the empty gap in the lower roofing.
When the height of the upper one was ten handbreadths or more. For in this case the upper one is considered a sukkah in its own right and invalidates the lower one.

And the roof of the lower one could bear cushions and pillows. The roof of the lower one, which is the floor of the upper one, is strong enough that one could place cushions and pillows on it for sleeping and sitting.
A canopy that has a roof. A covering around a bed that spreads over it.
And likewise one who sets up four posts. At the corners of the bed.
And spread a sheet over them. And the sheet slopes diagonally from the sides of the posts.
Even if they are any height at all. A very great measure.
For land cannot be stolen. Unlike movable property, land cannot pass into the possession and ownership of the robber (Hilchot Gezelah 8:14), and therefore in practice this is not a stolen sukkah.

And if he stole wood etc.. Although wood can be stolen, the Sages ordained that one who steals wood and uses it for a building need not demolish the building to return it but need only return its value (ibid. 1:5), and therefore the sukkah is valid.

And even if he stole boards and placed them and did not attach them etc.. Even when he did not attach the boards but merely placed them on the sukkah, the Sages ordained that if the owners come during the festival there is no obligation to dismantle the sukkah, but it suffices to pay their value (but after the festival he must return the boards to him - Hilchot Gezelah 1:5).
One who makes a sukkah in the public domain, it is valid. Even though this is not his ground.

Women and slaves... are exempt. For women are exempt from positive commandments that are time-bound (Hilchot Avodah Zarah 12:3), and a Canaanite slave is exempt from positive commandments from which women are exempt (Hilchot Chagigah 2:1).

A tumtum. One whose sexual organs are covered and it is not apparent whether he is male or female; if his sexual organs are revealed and he is found to be male, his law is that of a definite male, and if found to be female, she is a female (Hilchot Ishut 2:25).
And an androginos. One who has both male and female sexual organs, and is defined as a doubtful male, doubtful female whose sex there is no way to determine (ibid. 2:24).
One who is half slave and half free. One who had two partner owners and one of them freed him, or whose owner freed half of him (see Hilchot Avadim 7:4).
Who does not need his mother. Who does not call out for his mother when he wakes (Commentary on the Mishnah, Sukkah 2:7, based on Bavli 28b).
By the words of the scribes. By rabbinic enactment.
In order to train him in the mitzvot. See also above 2:7, Hilchot Megillah 1:1 and elsewhere.
And their attendants. Those who assist them.
Has a headache. His head hurts.
A mourner is obligated in sukkah. And he is not judged as one in distress, who is exempt from the sukkah.
And all the groomsmen. His friends who accompany him.
And all the members of the wedding canopy. Those who serve and assist in the joy of the wedding canopy.
Agents of a mitzvah. Those who travel from place to place for the sake of a mitzvah.
And his sukkah permanent. In which his main dwelling will be.
"You shall dwell in sukkot". That there will be your sitting and your dwelling.
And beautiful bedding. Fine fabrics and tablecloths.
Ashishot. Bottles or goblets.
But eating utensils such as pots and bowls, outside the sukkah. Because they are dirty and it is not respectful to the sukkah.

And if it was a small sukkah, he puts it outside the sukkah. Because the lamp is repulsive and unpleasant, and one should not bring it into a sukkah that is not spacious (Rashi, Sukkah 29a), or because the vapor of the lamp makes the air of the sukkah repulsive (and if so the law applies only to a burning lamp; Rabbenu Manoach). Some explain that there is concern that the sukkah will catch fire (Tosafot ibid.).

And even a casual sleep. Lest he fall asleep for a long time, or because with regard to sleep there is no definition of "casual," since even a little sleep may be significant for a particular person (both explanations are given in the Gemara, Sukkah 26a).

Like the law of eating matzah on Pesach. For there is an obligation to eat a kezayit of matzah on the first night of the festival, and on the other days of the festival one is not obligated to eat matzah (see Hilchot Chametz UMatzah 6:1).
And most of it. And most of his body.
And as if he did not eat in the sukkah. . And if this is the obligatory eating of the first night, he must eat again.
A decree lest he be drawn after his table. While eating he will draw himself toward the table and leave the area of the sukkah.
And even in a large sukkah. For even there they decreed lest he be drawn after his table.
Reads. Studies for the sake of fluency and review.
And when he understands and analyzes. He studies in depth what he learned, and needs a settled mind.
To leave. To leave the sukkah.
Even for a dish of beans. . Which spoils quickly.
He may not dismantle his sukkah. He may not take down the sukkah, since its mitzvah applies all day until evening.
He brings down his vessels. Back to the house, since from this time the house must be prepared in honor of the festival of Shemini Atzeret.
From Minchah time and onward. Toward evening, about two and a half hours before sunset and later.
He has no place to clear out. His vessels and to eat in them on Shemini Atzeret, and he wants to continue to eat in the sukkah.
He reduces it by four by four. From the roofing and invalidates it, so that it will be evident that its mitzvah has ended (below, halacha 14).
On the time. The blessing "Shehecheyanu" (see Hilchot Berachot 11:9).
And he arranges all the blessings over the cup. He recites these blessings in the order of the Kiddush over the cup of wine.
It turns out that he recites Kiddush standing etc.. So that he sits only after he blesses "to dwell in the sukkah."

In this time when we observe two days. Outside the Land of Israel the festival is observed for two days, as was done when they sanctified the month on the basis of sighting and there was doubt about the time the month was set (see Hilchot Kiddush HaChodesh 5:4-5). For this reason, on the eighth day of Sukkot one acts in one respect as if it were still Sukkot, and in another it is celebrated as Shemini Atzeret.
And we do not bless "to dwell in the sukkah". So that people will not come to treat lightly the day of Shemini Atzeret, which is exempt from sukkah (see Kesef Mishneh).
He brings a lamp into it. For it may not be brought into a small sukkah (above, halacha 5).
He brings pots and bowls and the like into it. For they are repulsive and may not be brought into a sukkah (ibid.).
In order to recognize that it is invalid and that its mitzvah is already completed. So that it will be evident that it is no longer sukkah time.
And he cannot reduce it and invalidate it. He cannot reduce the roofing (as above, halacha 11), since this is a festival on which the work of taking down is forbidden.
One may not benefit from them for anything else. One does not use them for other things apart from their use for the sukkah, since they were designated for a mitzvah.
All eight days. The seven days of the festival and Shemini Atzeret.
Designated. Set aside for the purpose of the mitzvah alone.

And since it was designated etc.. For the twilight period is doubtfully part of the seventh day and doubtfully part of the eighth night, and since use was forbidden at the beginning of the day because of the doubt, it is forbidden for all of it.
To make use. To use.
I do not set myself apart from them. I do not wish to separate myself and refrain from using them, thereby establishing that he does not want them to be designated for the mitzvah.
All of twilight. Of the eve of the first festival day.

For he did not designate them and the sanctity of the sukkah did not take effect on them and they were not considered like it. For by making a stipulation, they are no longer designated exclusively for the sukkah and are not considered part of it (but for the sukkah itself a stipulation does not help and its sanctity takes effect in any case).
The palm fronds mentioned in the Torah. In the command to take the four species on Sukkot.
Charyot. . Branches.
Before the leaves spread apart this way and that. While the leaves on the branch are closed and attached to it, before they begin to open outward to the sides.
A staff. Like a straight stick.
Whose leaves cover its wood. For the leaves cover and conceal the branch.
For example, that there be three leaves or more on one stalk. That at the point where the leaf connects to the branch ("stalk") at least three leaves grow.
A wild myrtle. Which is not straight and orderly.
Elongated. Lengthened and narrow.
And its edge is smooth. The edge of the leaf is smooth without protrusions.
And its stem. The branch.
Whose leaf is round. Rounded and not elongated.
And its edge resembles a saw. Serrated like a saw.
But it has small grooves etc.. The leaf is serrated but with very small protrusions, like a small sickle.
And all these matters. The identification of the four species.
From tradition. By tradition.
They are one mitzvah and they hold each other back. The mitzvah is fulfilled only when all the species are together.
And all of them are called the mitzvah of lulav. For the mitzvah is named after the lulav, as explained in the next halacha.
To bind. To tie together.
Since all of them are adjacent to it. All are named after the lulav, which is the largest and most prominent of them, and the other species are attached to it.
The way they grow. As they grow.
Their bases are down toward the earth and their tops are up toward the air. The end that attaches to the tree is down, and the other end is up.
One by one. Each one by itself, one after another.
Provided that all four of them are present with him. Are near him.
Willow branches. Branches of the willow.
And it is an adornment of the mitzvah. This adds beauty and splendor to the mitzvah.
And if he added or subtracted, he did not invalidate. This is the Rambam's final version; at first he wrote: "and if he added or subtracted it is invalid" (Responsa Birkat Avraham, no. 31).
Any length at all. However long.

And its measurement is from its spine only, not from the tip of the leaves. The length of the lulav is measured by the central branch from which the leaves emerge, and the ends of the leaves that extend beyond that are not taken into account.
Provided that he raises them in the way they grow. As explained above, halacha 6.
And he moves it out and back, up and down. He extends and returns the lulav to the sides, and extends the lulav upward and downward.
And he shakes the lulav three times in each direction. When he extends the lulav toward each of the directions, he shakes it three times.

How? etc.. He extends the lulav toward one of the directions, then shakes it three times, brings it back to himself and again shakes three times. Likewise in the other directions, and likewise upward and downward.
At the beginning and at the end. At the beginning of Psalm 118 and at its end.
Gimon. A grip strap.
Or he wrapped a sheet around it and took it. So that he did not take the lulav directly in his hands.
Taking by means of something else is called taking. Even though he took the four species with the help of something else, it is considered as if the person took them himself.
He separated them with myrtle leaves. That are not attached to the branch.
For one kind does not interpose with its own kind. And since the myrtle of the mitzvah and the myrtle leaves are of the same kind, there is no interposition here.
And he may. And he is permitted.
With a cord. A small measuring rope.

Since its binding is not essential. As above, halacha 6, and therefore the binding need not be specifically with one of the four species (see Bavli Sukkah 36b). And as for interposition, there is no problem since this is done for adornment.
Everywhere. In the Temple, in the Land of Israel and outside the Land.
And at all times. When the Temple stands and when it does not.
And in the Temple. Here it means all of Jerusalem (Commentary on the Mishnah, Sukkah 3:10, and see Piskim VeShitot).
"And you shall rejoice before the Lord your God seven days". From this we learn that the mitzvah on all seven days is specifically before the Lord - in the Temple.
Within the days of the festival. In the middle of the days of the festival and not on the first day.

A decree lest he carry it in his hand four cubits in the public domain. And this is work forbidden by the Torah (Hilchot Shabbat 12:8), and because of the concern about this prohibition they decreed that the positive commandment of lulav be set aside.
As we decreed for the shofar. Above 2:6; and see also Hilchot Megillah 1:13.

Because it is a mitzvah from the Torah, even in the outlying areas etc.. The mitzvah of taking on the first festival day is more stringent than on the other days, for unlike the other days, on the first festival day there is a mitzvah even in the outlying areas, and therefore they did not impose the decree on it.
In the outlying areas. Outside the Temple.
Because it is a mitzvah by rabbinic enactment. And one recites a blessing also on rabbinic mitzvot (Hilchot Berachot 11:3).
And this ordinance, with all the ordinances etc.. This ordinance is one of the ordinances that Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai enacted after the destruction (see also Hilchot Kiddush HaChodesh 3:6).
Matters will return to their former state. The law will return as it was before the destruction, and the lulav will be taken all seven days only in the Temple.

And likewise in the other places that knew etc.. When the court sanctified the month on the basis of sighting, they would send messengers to announce when the new month was set, and in distant places that the court's messengers did not reach, they would observe two festival days out of doubt (Hilchot Kiddush HaChodesh 5:4), and for this reason they would not take the lulav on the first day when it fell on Shabbat, since for them it was not certain that this was the first day of the festival.
On the first day. Also on the first day if it falls on Shabbat.
And even the people of the Land of Israel etc.. Who know without doubt when the new moon was.
The people of the distant outlying areas. The people of the distant countries.
So that everyone will be equal in this matter. So that there not be a situation where some take the lulav and some do not.

Since the obligation etc.. Since there is no longer any difference between one place and another, and one cannot rely on the fact that there is in any case a difference between the Temple and the provinces regarding the times for taking the lulav.

For everyone acts according to the calculation. For the fixing of the times is done according to a calculation set in advance and not on the basis of the court's sanctification of the month (see Hilchot Kiddush HaChodesh 5:2-3).
And even though everyone knows the fixing of the month. And everyone knows when Sukkot falls.
And we already explained. Above, halacha 13.
Anyone obligated in shofar and sukkah etc.. See above 2:1, 6:1.
A minor who knows how to shake. Who can hold the lulav and the species and shake them properly.
Branches. Branches.

And they stand them up against the sides of the altar with their tops bent over the altar. They stand them so that they lean against the wall of the altar and the ends of the branches lean over the altar itself. Afterwards they would take the willow and take it (below, halacha 22).
And they arrange. They stand it in the arrangement described.
They blow a tekiah, a teruah and a tekiah. With trumpets (compare Hilchot Kli HaMikdash 7:6).
Within the festival. At the beginning or middle of the days of the festival.
The seventh day. Of the festival.

In order to publicize that it is a mitzvah. For there were those who treated the willow lightly and claimed that it is not an obligation at all, and therefore, to show its importance, they ordained that it sometimes override Shabbat.
How did they do it?. . When the seventh day falls on Shabbat.
In golden basins. Filled with water.
Lest they wither. Lest they dry out.

And they take from it and take it as they do every day. From these willows that were brought while it was still day, they would take willow branches and take them in accordance with the mitzvah as every day.

For this is the custom of the prophets. . Taking the willow is a law given to Moses at Sinai, but according to the custom of the prophets they did not recite a blessing over it (Commentary on the Mishnah, Sukkah 4:3).
The ark. The holy ark in which the Torah scroll is placed (Hilchot Tefillah 11:3).
And when he enters the study hall. And will be busy with his learning and will not be able to give his attention to the lulav and hold it properly.
And returns it to the water on Shabbat. To keep it fresh, but it is forbidden to add to the water.
And on Chol HaMoed. The intermediate days of the festival.

Because it is fit only for smelling etc.. Since myrtle is used only for smelling, when it is designated for the mitzvah it is automatically forbidden for smelling. But the etrog, whose main use is for eating, when designated for the mitzvah is forbidden only for eating (see also above 6:16).
All of the seventh day. Even after they have taken it, and it will no longer be used for a mitzvah.

Because it was designated for part of the day, it was designated for all of it. Because it was designated for a mitzvah and was forbidden for other use for part of the day, it can no longer be permitted for use during the rest of that day (see also above 6:15).

And in this time when we observe two days. When they sanctified the month on the basis of sighting and those outside the Land did not know when the festival fell, they would observe it for two days out of doubt. And even now, when the festival is fixed according to the calendar calculation and there is no longer any doubt, the Sages ordained to continue the custom they previously followed of observing two days (see Hilchot Yom Tov 6:14, Hilchot Kiddush HaChodesh 5:4-5).
Even though the lulav is not taken on the eighth. For they did not ordain taking the lulav on it (unlike the sukkah, above 6:13; for the reason see Maggid Mishneh and Kesef Mishneh).

The etrog is forbidden on the eighth just as it was forbidden etc.. Since in the past the eighth day of Sukkot was possibly the seventh day, the etrog was forbidden for benefit on it. And although today there is no longer any doubt about the matter, the law has nevertheless not changed.
He fulfills his obligation with each one on its day and eats it the next day. For each etrog is forbidden only on the day for which it was set aside.

Even after despair. After its owner has given up hope of this object, since despair makes the object, for certain purposes, the property of the robber or thief (see Hilchot Genevah 1:11-12, 2:6, Hilchot Gezelah 2:2-3). And all these are invalid because it is a mitzvah performed through a transgression (Commentary on the Mishnah, Sukkah 3:1).
From an asherah that is worshipped. A tree planted to be used as an idol.

Even though they nullified the asherah from being worshipped. And the nullification permits its use (Hilchot Avodah Zarah 8:8), nevertheless they are invalid because before they nullified them their law was that they must be burned, and they were already rejected from serving for a mitzvah (Yad Peshutah).

An apostate city. A city most of whose inhabitants worshipped idols, all of whose property must be burned (Hilchot Avodah Zarah 4:6). For this reason the species coming from there are considered burned and as if lacking their measure explained above 7:8 (see Hilchot Shabbat 17:12; and see also above 1:3).
One of them was of idolatry. Which is idolatrous property and forbidden to benefit from, but there is no mitzvah to destroy it (R. Y. Kafih and Yad Peshutah).
And if he took it, he fulfilled his obligation. For mitzvot are not included in the category of benefit (see above 1:3).
It was withered but had not finished drying. It began to dry slightly but has not yet dried completely.

An etrog of orlah, of impure terumah, or of tevel is invalid. For the etrog is called "the fruit of a beautiful tree," and in all these cases the etrog is forbidden to eat (see Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 10:9, 10:19, Hilchot Terumot 7:3), and is not included in "fruit."

Demai. Produce of ignorant people, regarding which the Sages ordained that one who buys from them must separate tithes out of doubt (see Hilchot Ma'aser 9:1), but for the poor they permitted eating it as it is (ibid. 10:11).
Second tithe in Jerusalem. Whose law is that it is eaten in purity (Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 3:1).
Lest he make it susceptible to impurity. Lest he touch the etrog when his hands are wet and make it susceptible to receiving impurity (Hilchot Tum'at Ochalin 1:1-2).
Whose top was cut off. Its upper end was cut.
Split etc.. If its upper end was cut and separated into two parts noticeably distant from each other (so that it appears the lulav has two tops).
Bent forward. It bent so that its front side, where the spine of the lulav is, protrudes forward.
For this is its nature. For this is how lulavs grow naturally and normally.

Its leaves separated from one another but did not hang down like the leaves of palm fronds. The lulav leaves that are attached to the spine opened and separated from it and are no longer straight but stand slightly slanted, but did not hang down and fall completely, as happens with old palm branches.
The nature of the leaves of a lulav is so. This is how they grow.
They grow two by two and are attached at their backs. Each leaf is composed of a pair of leaves attached to each other on the side of the lulav's spine.
And the back of every two attached leaves. The length of the connection of each pair of leaves.
The twin was split. One of these connections separated.

Its leaves were not one on top of another as in all lulavs but one below another. A lulav whose leaves do not lie and rise partly one on top of the other as usual, but the tip of a leaf does not reach the base of the leaf following it.
If the top of this one reaches the base of the one above it. If the tip of the leaf reaches the place where the leaf above it begins.
If three leaves remained in one nest. If at least one point of attachment to the branch remained from which three leaves emerge (Tur Orach Chayim 646, see above 7:2; and see Piskim VeShitot).
Its berries were more than its leaves. The small fruits growing on the myrtle were more than the myrtle's leaves.
He reduced them. He removed some of the berries until they became a minority relative to the leaves.
For he is like one who repairs. Making the myrtle fit for use in the mitzvah resembles repairing a vessel, which is forbidden on Shabbat and festivals (see Hilchot Shabbat 23:8-9).
Or another picked them for eating. Whose intention was not to prepare the myrtle for the mitzvah but to eat the berries.
They were breached on it. As above, halacha 4.
A through hole. A hole from side to side.
And a hole that is not through etc.. And this is where the body of the etrog was not diminished (for example, where the flesh of the etrog was pushed inward and an indentation formed).
If it was like an issar. The size of a small coin.
Lacking anything at all. A little of the etrog's flesh was removed, even the slightest amount.
And it is the small head that has its blossom on it. The upper tip of the etrog ("pitam"), which is composed of a piece of wood with a kind of small circle ("shoshanah") on it.
The wood by which it hangs on the tree from the base of the etrog. The piece of wood at the lower end of the etrog that was attached to the etrog tree ("oketz").
Chazazit. A kind of small pustules.
On most of it. On most of the surface of the etrog.

Its outer layer was peeled, which does not diminish it but it remains etc.. The outer peel which, if removed, no deficiency would be noticeable in the etrog, but it would look green like a regular etrog.
Swollen. It became bloated.
Rotten. Foul-smelling and decayed.
Pickled. Soaked in vinegar or brine.
Boiled. Lightly cooked (see the explanation of Hilchot Chametz UMatzah 7:13).
Spotted. Of various colors.
Green as a leek. Dark green.
He grew it in a mold and made it like another creation. He put it, while still attached to the tree, into a mold so that it would grow inside it and take a form different from that of an etrog.

He made it like its natural form, even though he made it in panels. He put it into a mold whose shape is similar to the shape of an etrog and shaped it squared and not round as it is naturally (Rabbenu Chananel), or it means he shaped it with protrusions, like a cogwheel (Rashi).
The twin. Two etrogim stuck together, or it means an etrog whose upper part is completely divided into two separate halves joined together only at its bottom.
And the unripe one. That has not yet ripened for eating.
A kind of slight blackness. Slightly dark, but not dark black.
Everywhere. Even if etrogim grow this way in that place.
On the first festival day only. On which the mitzvah of lulav is from the Torah.
And the disqualification that is due to idolatry. An asherah and an apostate city.
Whether on the first festival day or on the other days it is invalid. Because they are considered as if they do not exist (see above, halacha 1).

Until he gives it to him as a gift. For on the first day the lulav must belong to him, as the Torah commands "you shall take for yourselves on the first day" (Leviticus 23:40), and it is derived: "for yourselves" - that it be yours.
He gave it to him on condition to return it. He gave him a gift on condition that in the end he return the gift to him.
For a gift on condition to return is called a gift. See also Hilchot Zechiyah UMatanah 3:9.

For a minor acquires but does not transfer to others by Torah law etc.. By Torah law a minor can acquire an object and become its owner (see ibid. 4:7), but cannot transfer his object to others (see Hilchot Mechirah 29:1). Therefore when a person gives him his lulav as a gift he acquires it, and he cannot transfer it back to its original owner.
Who bought etrogim from the house's holdings. From an inheritance that fell to them and which they had not yet divided among themselves ("the house's holdings"), and they bought etrogim with it.

If he can eat it etc.. If he can eat this etrog without it bothering the other brothers, it is considered as if he bought this etrog entirely from his share of the inheritance, and it is entirely his and he fulfills his obligation with it.

And if this one bought an etrog and that one a parish, or they bought as one etc.. If with the inheritance money (before the division) one of the brothers bought an etrog and the other a pomegranate or a parish (quince), or all of them together bought with this money an etrog and a pomegranate or a parish.

He does not fulfill his obligation with the etrog until he gives him his share as a gift, even though if he ate it they would not object. For although they do not object if he ate it, nevertheless the etrog is not acquired by him for his share of the inheritance until they explicitly transfer it to him, because it differs from other fruits in that it is used for a mitzvah (see Yad Peshutah).
It is a mitzvah to rejoice in them. See Hilchot Yom Tov 6:17-21.
"And you shall rejoice before the Lord your God seven days". So Scripture added a special mitzvah to rejoice all seven days of the festival before the Lord - in the Temple.
After they offer the afternoon tamid. At nine and a half seasonal hours from the beginning of the day (Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 1:3).
Strikes. Plays an instrument.
And one who knows by mouth, by mouth. One who knows how to sing with his mouth sings with his mouth.
And they clap. They strike percussion instruments (Commentary on the Mishnah, Beitzah 5:2).
And they clap hands. They clap their hands (ibid.).

It does not override either Shabbat or a festival. Because this rejoicing involves things forbidden on Shabbat and festivals (such as playing, striking and clapping, see Hilchot Shabbat 23:4-5), and they did not permit them for this purpose.
For the rejoicing with which a person rejoices in the performance of mitzvot etc.. And therefore it is a mitzvah to increase in this rejoicing and not to diminish its importance.

"Because you did not serve the Lord your God with joy and gladness of heart". . This is stated in the passage of rebuke as the reason for Israel's punishment, and the verse is interpreted to mean that the sin for which they will be punished is that they did not serve God with joy.
One who is arrogant, grants himself honor and is honored in his own eyes. Who is haughty and considers himself so honored that it is not fitting for him to lower himself and dance and leap.
Do not glorify yourself before a king. Do not be proud and consider yourself honored when you are before the King - the Holy One, blessed be He.

He is the great and honored one who serves out of love. Who does not act for his own benefit but for the sake of Heaven, and thereby expresses his great love for the Holy One, blessed be He (see Hilchot Teshuvah chapter 10).

"And I will be yet more lightly esteemed than this, and I will be lowly in my own eyes". So David said to Michal his wife after she accused him of leaping and whirling before the Ark of the Lord when they brought it up to Jerusalem (II Samuel chapter 6).
